prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level and opened new precision tests of fundamental physics.

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep a single-part prize on the optical lattice clock, B053, with Katori and Ye, and my configuration is unchanged from round 1. The scientific point that persuades me is that the magic-wavelength lattice is a new regime and not a refinement: it cancels the light shift of the clock transition while the atoms are held tightly enough to remove Doppler and recoil effects, and it lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once. That is what made 1e-18 systematic uncertainty and very high stability reachable, and the performance has been reproduced and compared across independent laboratories, which is the robustness test I care most about. The same clocks now resolve gravitational redshift over millimetre scales, constrain drifts of constants and anchor the roadmap for the second. Katori's concept and first demonstrations together with Ye's accuracy and many-body advances give a clean two-name credit that fits well inside the three-person limit. I note that nobody in round 1 disputed the pair; the open questions were priority history and overlap, and neither changes my view of the science.
statement.case_against: The reservations I take seriously are these. Ye shared the 2005 prize and the 2012 prize rewarded ion control and clocks, so a third metrology prize with a repeat laureate needs a citation that isolates the lattice concept instead of 'better clocks'. The pending SI redefinition and the Sr-lattice priority history (Tokyo, JILA, SYRTE, PTB, NIST, and contributors such as Lemonde, Ludlow and Hall) have not been checked against the record by this committee, and I cannot settle them myself. Ulf Danielsson's point that the fundamental tests so far are null results is fair: the discovery being rewarded is a measurement capability and a controlled quantum many-body system, not a new law. I accept that and would phrase the citation accordingly. Finally, clocks are adjacent to my field, so I defer to Eva Lindroth and Stefan Kroll on atomic details.

responses.point: Ulf prefers B046, the experimental Higgs discovery, as the most secure and central result on the list, but concedes that the attribution is very hard and that a clock prize would be the more defensible choice if no trio can be justified. He also asks what has been learned about nature from clock tests that so far give null results.
responses.response: I agree the Higgs observation is scientifically the heavier result, and I do not think the 2013 theory prize closes the experimental credit. My difficulty is exactly the one he states. Two collaborations of thousands, four credible names and three different trios proposed around this table (his, mine in the opening, and the Chair's) tell me that any choice would be contested on the record, and I am not a particle physicist, so I defer to him on the science but not on whether a trio is defensible. On his null-result question, I would answer that precision experiments often reward the instrument that makes a new regime accessible. The clock does more than bound constants: it is the first system where the gravitational redshift is seen across a millimetre and where many-body effects in the lattice are controlled and used. I keep B046 as an alternative for that reason, and I would revisit it if the expert reports gave a principled trio.

responses.point: Bernhard prefers B013, Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, as a mature theory-plus-experiment prize with a stable interpretation after fifteen years. He accepts that omitting Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 2016 prize are genuine reservations.
responses.response: I agree that it is the cleanest narrative among the condensed-matter entries and that the Z2 idea is general. But I still weigh the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang more heavily than he does, because their proposal is what pointed Molenkamp to HgTe, and the three-person limit leaves no room. The 2016 citation was broad enough that I expect a fraction of the Academy to read B013 as a continuation. Hasan's strand is a separable second story, so the committee would have to choose between a narrow 2D citation and an arbitrary exclusion. If he would accept restricting the citation to the quantum spin Hall effect, I would support B013 as the strongest condensed-matter fallback, which is why I keep it as my first alternative. It does not displace B053 for me, because the clock has no equivalent attribution hole.

responses.point: Eva prefers B052, aberration-corrected electron microscopy with Rose, Urban and Haider, as a statutory invention that removed the Scherzer limit and is now routine, while flagging the uncredited STEM work of Krivanek, Dellby and Lupini and thin opening support.
responses.response: The statutory word invention is a fair point, and the impact on atomic-scale characterisation of quantum materials, including superconducting-device materials I care about, is real. It is also the case that for an instrument the test is whether it is reproducible, and here it clearly is. My hesitation is the attribution she herself identifies. The TEM and STEM correctors were developed in parallel, and a citation that credits only the TEM route could read as incomplete, while adding the STEM names breaks the three-person limit. I also see the clock as having a stronger discovery component in the fundamental tests it enables. I would be glad to see the expert report on the TEM/STEM priority history, and if it cleanly supports her trio I would treat B052 as a serious candidate for a later year, but I do not move it ahead of B053 now.

responses.point: Mark, as Chair, moved to B053 because attribution, maturity and measurement quality line up, but flags the pending SI redefinition and the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes as reasons for caution, and asks for expert reports on the Sr-lattice priority history.
responses.response: I share his assessment and I answer his two concerns directly. On the redefinition, I would not wait: the Prize rewards demonstrated performance, which has been independently confirmed, and the redefinition is a metrological decision downstream of the evidence. On the overlap, I would resist treating the 2005 and 2012 prizes as a bar. The frequency comb prize recognised a different tool, and the 2012 prize recognised control of single trapped ions. The lattice clock is a distinct achievement, because neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice give a different noise and systematics regime. I support his request for expert reports before names are fixed, and I would ask that they specifically test whether Katori and Ye are sufficient, since the whole case for B053 rests on that.

uncertainties: Whether the expert reports on Sr-lattice priority show that Katori and Ye are a sufficient pair, or that another contributor must be considered inside the three-person limit.
Whether the committee accepts Ye as a repeat laureate for a third precision-metrology prize, and whether the citation can isolate the magic-wavelength lattice from the 2005 and 2012 achievements.
Whether the Higgs experimental credit (B046) can be allocated to three names in a way the committee can defend; I am not the right member to judge that.
Whether a second part (for example B013 or B046) would improve the prize, given that any second part consumes at most one person under the three-person limit and I see no candidate for that slot.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work in superconducting circuits at Chalmers, so I remain closely proximate to B001 (circuit QED). I will recuse myself from any decision on B001 and disclose this again here, although B001 is no longer in my configuration or alternatives. Mehlig has noted institutional Gothenburg ties to me and Olsson, and I note that Olsson is a Chalmers colleague whose field (electron microscopy, B052) I do not work in. I know of no personal tie to Katori, Ye or the B013, B046 candidates beyond the normal scientific one.
